title: Although, even, on the contrary
goal: Express contrast and concession with the right word for the job: *walaupun* and *meskipun* for “although”, *padahal* for “even though (and it shouldn't be so)”, *bahkan* for “even”, *malah* and *justru* for “on the contrary”, and *namun* for a formal “however”.
bekal: use *padahal* to show that reality has let you down
tell *bahkan*, *malah* and *justru* apart and use each in its place

notes: **Walaupun sudah pesan… airnya dingin** — *walaupun* and *meskipun* both mean “although” and are interchangeable. Their short forms *walau* and *meski* are common in writing and headlines. The clause can go first or second: *Airnya dingin walaupun saya sudah pesan air panas.*

**Padahal** is “even though” with a sigh built in: the fact that follows makes the situation more annoying or surprising. Bu Ratna is not just giving information; she is sharing the guest's frustration. Unlike *walaupun*, *padahal* always comes **second**, after the disappointing fact.

**Bahkan** — “even”, used to add a stronger point to a list: bad water, **and even** power cuts. It usually opens the sentence or stands right before the surprising element: *Bahkan anak kecil pun tahu.*

**Meskipun sudah kami tegur** — Bu Ratna's joke works because *menegur* (to reprimand, have a word with) is something you do to people. Humour is a standard way to calm a complaint in Indonesia; a smile is worth more than a long apology.

**Justru lebih kecil** — *justru* says “in fact, precisely the opposite of what you expect”. Pak Wijaya expected bigger; it is smaller. Compare *malah* in line 13: the guest who came to complain ends up feeling bad himself — an outcome that went the other way.
**Maklum** — “I understand (and forgive)”, said about things you can't reasonably expect otherwise: *Maklum, desa* (“well, it's a village”). *Mohon maklum* on a notice means “please bear with us”.

grammars.title: Although: walaupun, meskipun, sekalipun, padahal
body: The first three introduce a fact that does **not** stop the main clause from being true. *Padahal* does the reverse: it adds the fact that makes the main clause surprising or unfair.
after: ⚠️ Do not use *tetapi* after a *walaupun* clause: *Walaupun hujan, tetapi tamu datang* is a classic error in formal writing (it is two conjunctions for one link). Use *tetap* (“still”) in the main clause instead: *Walaupun hujan, tamu tetap datang.*
*Padahal* can also stand alone as a reply, with a sigh: “Airnya dingin.” — “*Padahal* sudah bayar mahal…” (“And I paid so much, too…”).

grammars.title: bahkan, malah, justru: three kinds of surprise
body: All three are often translated “even” or “in fact”, which is why learners mix them up. Each one points at a different kind of surprise.

head: Word
The surprise
Example
English
rows: goes further in the same direction
treated, and it got worse instead
precisely the opposite of what was assumed
it was actually him who apologised
I ended up being treated, of all things
that's precisely why we need rules

after: A quick test: if you could say “and what's more”, use *bahkan*. If you could say “instead”, use *malah*. If you could say “it's precisely the reverse” or “that's exactly the point”, use *justru*.
💬 *Malah* is also a common grumble on its own: *Lho, malah pergi!* — “What, he just left!”

dialogs.intro: Monday morning at the Yogya office. A short video Mas Bayu made about Sumberwangi has spread across social media over the weekend, and nobody is more surprised than Sarah.

notes: **Kok bisa?** — the title of this scene — is the standard “how on earth?”. *Kok* marks surprise at something that should not have happened, or not like that. Unit 14 gives the particles a full table.

**…to** — at the end of a sentence in Central Java, *to* (from Javanese *ta*) asks for agreement, like *kan* or English “you know”, “right?”. Mas Bayu uses it constantly; standard Indonesian would use *kan* or *bukan*.
**Konten mahal-mahal** — the doubled adjective means “all that expensive stuff”, with a touch of irony. Doubling to suggest “all sorts of, the whole lot” is the A2 Unit 8 pattern put to work.

**Dibuat-buat** — “made up, put on, not genuine”. *Senyumnya dibuat-buat* is a forced smile. Its opposite is *apa adanya*, “just as it is”, a phrase Indonesians use approvingly about people, food and videos alike.

**Namanya juga rezeki** — *rezeki* is one's God-given share of good fortune or income. *Namanya juga…* (“well, it's called …”) is the shrug of acceptance: *Namanya juga anak-anak* (“kids will be kids”).

**Tiga kali lipat** — “threefold”. *Lipat* means “fold”; *dua kali lipat* is double, *sepuluh kali lipat* tenfold. *Omong-omong* (“by the way”) is the spoken twin of *ngomong-ngomong*; in chat it is shortened to *btw*.

grammars.title: tetapi, namun, sedangkan: joining two sides
body: When the contrast is between two whole statements, choose by register and by what is being compared.

head: Connector
Where
Register
Example
rows: *Yoga bikin konten mahal, sedangkan Bayu cuma lima menit.*

after: ⚠️ Editors prefer *namun* or *akan tetapi*, not *tetapi*, at the start of a written sentence. In speech nobody minds *Tapi…* at the beginning.
*Sedangkan* is only for comparing two different things side by side (“whereas”). It cannot introduce a single contrast on its own.

sections.title: padahal: the word with a sigh in it

blocks.text: *Padahal* is one of the most Indonesian words there is, and one of the hardest to translate. It introduces the fact that makes the situation unfair, ironic or disappointing. English uses “and yet”, “even though”, “when in fact” or just a tone of voice.

head: Indonesian
English
rows: He didn't come, even though he'd promised.
It's raining again, and it was sunny a moment ago.
*Mas Bayu bilang capek, padahal belum kerja.*
Bayu says he's tired, when he hasn't done any work yet.
And I paid a lot, too.
The price went up, yet the quality's the same.
*Kamu kok diam saja? Padahal kamu yang tahu.*
Why are you so quiet? You're the one who knows.

blocks.text: ⚠️ Do not use *padahal* for a neutral “although”. *Padahal hujan, saya pergi* is wrong; that is *Walaupun hujan, saya tetap pergi.* *Padahal* looks back at something that ought to have changed the outcome and did not.

blocks.title: padahal or walaupun?
items: *Walaupun capek, dia tetap bekerja.* — a fact that did not stop something (neutral).
*Dia bilang capek, padahal belum bekerja.* — a fact that shows something is not as it should be (complaint, irony).
If you can add “and yet, come on!” to the English, *padahal* is probably right.

blocks.text: Reports, news and speeches use a small set of fixed phrases to concede a point before moving on. Recognising them makes formal texts much easier to follow.

items: *Kendati diguyur hujan, festival tetap ramai.* — Although it poured, the festival was still busy.
*Terlepas dari kekurangannya, program ini berhasil.* — Whatever its shortcomings, the programme succeeded.
*Nggak apa-apa, toh cuma sehari.* — It's fine, it's only one day after all.

blocks.text: *Kendati* is a favourite of headline writers because it is short and sounds serious. In conversation it would sound like reading the news aloud; stick to *walaupun* and *meskipun*.
Cover the Indonesian column, read the English, and rebuild each sentence from memory.

To be honest, I'm still not quite convinced. Local people shouldn't be treated the same as tourists.
